f1stra:361: The context window is all the content the model can "see" at once when generating the next response. It includes your system prompt, previous conversation, every tool call and its output, and every file you have read. Claude Code has a context window of up to **1 million tokens**. Unfortunately, using context carries an implicit cost, often called **context rot**. This phenomenon means that as the context grows, model performance declines. Because attention is spread across too many tokens, stale and irrelevant content begins to interfere with completing the current task. The context window is a "hard limit". When you approach the window limit, you need to summarize the current task into a shorter description and continue working in a new context window—we call this **compaction**. You can also trigger compaction manually.

z6vif6:304: Claude Code's 1M token context window appears on the surface to be a "generous" limit, but the article reveals a counterintuitive reality: the more context there is, the worse the model performs. This phenomenon is called "Context Rot," and its underlying mechanism is attention dispersion—when the amount of information the model needs to process exceeds its optimal processing threshold, valuable signals are drowned out by noise. Notably, the article does not describe context rot as a defect that can be completely eliminated through engineering means, but rather positions it as an "implicit cost"—an honest acknowledgment of the inherent limitations of LLMs in long-context scenarios. The existence of the 1M limit is itself a hard constraint. When approaching that limit, users are forced to perform compression operations, which means context rot is not a question of whether it occurs, but when it occurs.
